subject: physics
title: Background radiation
key_idea: **Background radiation** is nuclear radiation that is around us all the time. It comes from natural sources, such as rocks and cosmic rays, and from man-made sources, such as nuclear accidents. The dose a person receives depends on where they live and work.

blocks.text: Background radiation is always present, even when no radioactive source is near. This section covers where it comes from.

items.meaning: Nuclear radiation that is around us all of the time.
A source that is part of the environment, whatever people do.
A source that exists because of human activity.

items: **Rocks** and the ground, including radon gas
**Cosmic rays** from space and the Sun
Food and water
Buildings
Fallout from **nuclear weapons testing**
**Nuclear accidents**, such as Chernobyl or Fukushima
Medical uses, such as X-rays and radiotherapy
Nuclear waste and nuclear power stations

diagram.alt: Sort sources of background radiation into natural and man-made.
diagram.prompt: Is each source of background radiation natural or man-made?

items: Background radiation is around us all the time.
Natural sources include rocks, radon gas and cosmic rays.
Man-made sources include nuclear accidents, nuclear weapons testing and medical X-rays.

blocks.text: A person's dose measures the radiation they absorb and the risk of harm it causes. Dose is measured in sieverts (Sv), and 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 Sv.
Dose depends on **location** and on **occupation**. Some rocks give out more radiation than others, so people in some places receive a higher dose.

items: Pilots receive extra dose from cosmic rays while flying.
Nuclear power station workers are exposed to nuclear radiation.
Granite worktops give out a small dose every day.

blocks.label: Total dose
blocks.formula: total dose = dose per day × number of days
where: dose per day in millisieverts per day (mSv/day)

items.text: A granite worktop gives 0.003 mSv per day.
The lowest dose with evidence of causing cancer is 100 mSv, so 1.095 mSv is far below it.

items: Dose is measured in sieverts. 1000 mSv = 1 Sv.
Location and occupation change a person's dose.
Compare a calculated dose with a harmful dose to judge the risk.

blocks.text: A Geiger-Muller tube and counter detects radiation. It also detects background radiation, so a reading is always too high.

blocks.label: Corrected count rate
blocks.formula: corrected count rate = measured count rate − background count rate
where: all count rates in counts per second (counts/s), or all in counts per minute (counts/min)
count rate = number of counts ÷ time

items: A reading is still above zero when the source is taken away.
This is because of background radiation.

diagram.alt: Correct a measured count rate for background radiation.
diagram.question: A Geiger-Muller tube records {counts} counts in 60 seconds from a rock. The background count rate is {bg} counts per second. Calculate the corrected count rate in counts per second.
working: Measured count rate = {counts} ÷ 60 counts per second
Corrected count rate = measured count rate − {bg}

items: A detector reads above zero without a source because of background radiation.
Subtract the background count rate from the measured count rate.
Use the same unit for both rates before subtracting.

checks.q: Give two natural sources and two man-made sources of background radiation.
checks.a: Natural: any two from rocks, radon gas, cosmic rays. Man-made: any two from nuclear accidents, nuclear weapons testing, medical X-rays, radiotherapy.

checks.q: A detector counts 540 counts in 60 seconds from a source. The background count rate is 0.40 counts per second. Calculate the corrected count rate.
checks.a: Measured count rate = 540 ÷ 60 = 9.0 counts per second. Corrected count rate = 9.0 − 0.40 = 8.6 counts per second.

checks.q: A worker receives 0.002 mSv each day. Calculate their dose after 30 days.
Explain why a detector still gives a reading when the radioactive source has been taken away.
checks.a: It is detecting background radiation, which is around us all the time.

exam_phrases: (well) below the lowest dose with evidence of causing cancer / harm
people are able to compare a radiation risk / dose / hazard to the radiation dose from (eating) bananas

mistakes.wrong: The count rate for the rock is 819 ÷ 60 + 0.30 = 13.95 counts per second.
mistakes.right: Background radiation is subtracted, not added: 13.65 − 0.30 = 13.35 counts per second. The answer 13.95 scores 2 of the 3 marks.

mistakes.wrong: Radioactive waste from nuclear power stations is another man-made source of background radiation.
mistakes.right: When waste is already given, it is ignored. Name another source, such as medical X-rays, radiotherapy, nuclear weapons testing or a named nuclear accident.

mistakes.wrong: The dose is 0.003 mSv, which is a small number, so the householder is safe.
mistakes.right: Work out the yearly dose (0.003 × 365 = 1.095 mSv), then compare it with the lowest dose with evidence of causing cancer (100 mSv).

worked_example.question: Workers in the nuclear power industry are exposed to nuclear radiation. Pilots on aircraft are exposed to cosmic radiation from space. The daily dose caused by working in a nuclear power station is 0.00050 mSv. The hourly dose from cosmic rays to a pilot while flying is 0.0030 mSv. Calculate the number of days it takes for a nuclear power station worker to receive the same dose as a pilot flying for 24 hours.
worked_example.tip: Convert the pilot's hourly dose to a daily dose first. Then divide by the worker's daily dose.

mistakes.wrong: Two sources of background radiation are alpha and beta radiation.
mistakes.right: Alpha, beta and gamma are ignored. They are types of radiation, not sources. Name a source, such as cosmic rays, rocks or radon.

mistakes.wrong: The detector still gives a reading because the source is not completely removed.
mistakes.right: Give the reason that the reading is not zero: background radiation. A named source of background radiation is also accepted.

worked_example.question: State two sources of background radiation.
answer_points: Any two from: cosmic rays, the Sun, rocks or the ground, nuclear tests or nuclear waste, nuclear power stations, plants, buildings, food, water, medical sources, radon.
Nuclear accidents, named foods, X-rays and radiotherapy are also accepted.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each source. Alpha, beta and gamma are ignored.
